passage: Madhav ran a small agricultural supply shop in a town near Hubli. His phone buzzed all day with group chats, videos and news alerts. One evening he realised he'd spent two hours watching short clips and forgotten to call a farmer back about seeds. His friend Eshaan, a schoolteacher, had deleted most apps from his own phone. "I kept only what I need," Eshaan said. "Business chat, bank, weather." Madhav tried it. He muted twenty groups, deleted the video app and put his phone in a drawer after nine. The first week felt restless; he kept reaching for it. By the third week he'd read half a book on soil health. Business calls got returned the same day.

qa.q: How long had Madhav spent watching short clips that evening?
qa.a: He had spent two hours watching them.

qa.q: What does Madhav keep reaching for his phone in the first week suggest?
qa.a: It suggests his habit was strong and he felt restless without constant updates.

qa.q: What made Madhav's changes effective?
qa.a: He removed apps he didn't need, muted distracting groups and set a time for the phone to go away.

qa.q: How might the farmers Madhav works with see this change?
qa.a: They'd likely notice he calls back faster and seems more attentive, which builds trust. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young shopkeeper choosing his technology deliberately instead of by default.

passage: Kaito, a graphic designer in Osaka, noticed he checked the news every time he waited for a file to render. He felt anxious and scattered by lunchtime. His colleague Nadia had a different system: she read one weekly news summary on Sunday and nothing else. "Isn't that out of touch?" Kaito asked. "I miss nothing important," she said. "Important things are still there on Sunday." Kaito tried a milder version. He removed news apps, kept one trusted source he read in the evening, and set his phone to grayscale during work. The first days he felt left out of office chatter. After a month, he found he could hold a design idea in his head for an hour without losing it.

qa.q: When does Nadia read her weekly news summary?
qa.a: She reads it on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Kaito feel before changing his habits?
qa.a: He felt anxious and scattered by lunchtime from checking news constantly.

qa.q: What choices did Kaito make to use technology more deliberately?
qa.a: He removed news apps, kept one trusted source for evenings and set his phone to grayscale at work.

qa.q: How does Nadia see keeping up with the news?
qa.a: She believes important news will still be there on Sunday, so constant checking isn't necessary.

grounding: Shows a young designer choosing his information diet consciously after seeing a colleague's approach.

passage: At the engineering firm's weekly team meeting, Vaibhav noticed everyone, including himself, was typing on laptops while someone presented. Nobody remembered decisions afterward. As the newest team lead, he proposed an experiment: laptops closed in meetings except for the note-taker, and messages answered in two batches a day instead of instantly. Akash, the senior engineer, scoffed. "Clients expect quick replies." "Urgent calls still come through," Vaibhav said. "Let's try two weeks." The first week was awkward; people fidgeted. By the second, meetings ended fifteen minutes early. Akash admitted he'd finished a design he'd been stuck on for a month. He didn't say thanks. But he started closing his laptop without being asked.

qa.q: How often would messages be answered in Vaibhav's experiment?
qa.a: They would be answered in two batches a day.

qa.q: Why did Akash scoff at the proposal at first?
qa.a: He worried that clients would be unhappy if replies weren't quick.

qa.q: What made Vaibhav's experiment easier for the team to accept?
qa.a: He framed it as a short two-week trial and kept urgent calls open, so people didn't feel cut off.

qa.q: How did Akash's view seem to change?
qa.a: After finishing a stuck design, he quietly began closing his laptop in meetings, showing he saw the benefit.

grounding: Shows a young team lead introducing deliberate tech habits at work and colleagues slowly adopting them.

passage:
Dear Bhavna,
You asked what happened with my 'phone experiment', so here's the full report. In September I noticed I picked up my phone about a hundred times a day, mostly without deciding to. So I did an audit: I listed every app and asked, 'Did I choose this, or did it choose me?' I kept maps, banking, messages, my music and the reading app. Deleted the rest, including two social apps I'd had since college. I moved email to the laptop only, checked twice a day. On weekends I use Nani's old keypad phone. The first week I kept reaching for a phone that wasn't there, honestly twitchy. By week three I'd finished two novels and restarted my sketchbook. I haven't become a monk. I still watch shows, but I choose them now. Want to try it with me in November?
Love,
Minakshi

qa.q: What question did Minakshi ask about each app?
qa.a: 'Did I choose this, or did it choose me?'

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel in the first week, and what does it show?
qa.a: Twitchy and restless, reaching for a phone that was not there, which shows how automatic the habit had become.

qa.q: Which of Minakshi's choices made that technology use more deliberate?
qa.a: Auditing the apps, deleting ones not really chosen, moving email to the laptop at set times, and using a keypad phone on weekends.

qa.q: How might Bhavna react to the invitation to try it in November?
qa.a: Probably curious, since Minakshi's results were real but balanced rather than preachy 😊

grounding: A letter shows a young adult auditing their apps and choosing tools and information diet deliberately.

passage: 'Abhinav bhai, how do you leave work so calm?' Irfan, the short version? I used to have eleven tools open at work and felt busy all day without finishing anything. Chat, email, three project boards, news tabs. One evening I realised I couldn't name a single thing I'd done that day that mattered. So I started choosing on purpose. I asked my team if we could agree on one place for tasks instead of three. That took a meeting and some grumbling, but we did it. I turned off all notifications except direct messages from my manager and two teammates. News I now read once, at lunch, from two sources I picked, not from whatever the feed pushes. And my phone stays in my bag during deep-work blocks. Honestly, the hardest part was the fear of missing something. I've missed almost nothing. And I leave work with a quieter head.

qa.q: How many tools did Abhinav used to have open at work?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: What was the hardest part for Abhinav, and what does it show?
qa.a: The fear of missing something, which shows how closely his default tech habits were tied to anxiety.

qa.q: What changes made Abhinav's technology use deliberate?
qa.a: Agreeing on one task tool, limiting notifications to key people, reading news at lunch from chosen sources, and keeping his phone away during deep work.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's team have felt about switching to one task tool?
qa.a: Some grumbled at first, but they probably benefit from less scattered work too.

grounding: A young professional describes consciously choosing his work tools and information sources instead of living by default.

passage: I'm Disha, Baljeet's flatmate. Last year she went through what I called her "phone diet". I don't know everything she was thinking; I saw what she did. One Sunday she sat at the dining table with her phone and a notebook, deleting apps one by one and writing down why she kept the rest: maps, banking, the family chat, a meditation timer. Fourteen apps went. Then she bought a cheap basic phone and carried only that on Saturdays. The first Saturday she kept patting her pocket. By the fourth she was reading novels on the balcony and calling her Nani instead of texting. She kept one news subscription she paid for and dropped the free feeds. She still used her laptop for work, of course. She just decided what came into her day. I copied half of it. I'm still not brave enough for the basic phone.

qa.q: How many apps did Baljeet delete?
qa.a: Fourteen apps.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling on the first Saturday with the basic phone?
qa.a: Baljeet seemed restless and uneasy, patting a pocket and missing the old habit.

qa.q: What made Baljeet's approach deliberate rather than simply cutting back?
qa.a: She wrote a reason for every app she kept, chose a paid news source over free feeds, and set a regular phone-light day.

qa.q: How does Disha see the change?
qa.a: Disha admires it enough to copy half of it, though not yet brave enough for the basic phone.

grounding: A flatmate describes a young woman choosing her apps and information sources deliberately.

passage:
March. Mehak's phone buzzed ninety times on an ordinary Tuesday: work chat, email, three shopping apps, a news app, the building group. She answered her manager Nandini's messages at 11 p.m. because the notification was there. She felt busy all the time and did nothing deep.
April. After forgetting a friend's birthday dinner, she spent a Saturday deciding what deserved her attention. Notifications off for everything except calls and family. Work chat only on the laptop, only between nine and seven. News once a day, in the evening. She told Nandini, nervously, "If something is urgent after seven, please call me." Nandini said, "Honestly, I'll do the same."
June. Mehak's phone buzzed eleven times on a Tuesday. She finished a report she had dodged for weeks in one long morning. Nandini called her after seven only once, for a real emergency, and Mehak didn't mind at all.

qa.q: How many times did Mehak's phone buzz on a Tuesday in June?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling when she asked Nandini to call if something was urgent?
qa.a: Mehak felt nervous about how Nandini would react to the new limits.

qa.q: Which choices made Mehak's technology use deliberate?
qa.a: Turning off notifications except calls and family, keeping work chat to laptop hours, and reading news once a day.

qa.q: How does Nandini respond to Mehak's limit?
qa.a: Nandini welcomes it and adopts it herself, calling after hours only for a real emergency.

grounding: Over three months, a young professional replaces default notifications with deliberate choices about attention.

passage: Sabina, you say you can't stop scrolling the news. Let your Hansa Khala tell you something from before phones. When I was twenty-five, working at a newspaper in Hyderabad, the new cable channels arrived with news all day and all night. I kept the TV on from waking to sleeping, afraid to miss anything. I felt informed and exhausted, and I started snapping at people. One evening my editor, a grey-haired man called Mr Qadri, said, "Hansa, you're reading everything and thinking nothing." That stung. So I made rules. TV news once, at nine. One good newspaper, read with a pen. Anything I repeated at work, I checked with a second source first. My head cleared. My writing got better. Now you carry a hundred cable channels in your pocket. Same choice, Sabina. Decide what comes in, or it decides for you.

qa.q: Where did Hansa work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At a newspaper in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What was young Hansa feeling when Mr Qadri said she was reading everything and thinking nothing?
qa.a: Hansa felt stung and hurt, but it made her rethink her habits.

qa.q: What rules did Hansa make, and why did they help?
qa.a: News on TV once at nine, one good newspaper read with a pen, and a second source before repeating anything; they turned endless intake into focused thinking.

qa.q: How might Mr Qadri have seen young Hansa?
qa.a: Mr Qadri probably saw a capable young journalist wearing herself out, and cared enough to say it bluntly.

grounding: An aunt tells a young woman how, at twenty-five, she chose her news diet deliberately instead of by default.

passage:
Ujjwal had a book translation due in ten days, a flatmate who practised the drums, and wifi that dropped every hour. The one thing that never dropped was his phone: three news apps, four social feeds, and a dozen group chats buzzing all day.

On Monday he counted: he had checked his phone ninety times before lunch.

That night he made choices, not rules. He kept one news source, read once in the morning. He deleted two feeds entirely and moved the others off his home screen. He left six group chats and muted five. He kept the family chat.

The drums were harder. He asked Tenzin to practise after seven, and Tenzin agreed if Ujjwal bought the earplugs.

The next week, the wifi still dropped. But when it did, Ujjwal kept translating from the printed pages. He finished two days early, and on the last evening he went to Tenzin's gig without taking a single photo.

qa.q: How many times had Ujjwal checked his phone before lunch on Monday?
qa.a: He had checked his phone ninety times before lunch.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt after counting ninety checks?
qa.a: Ujjwal was probably shocked and frustrated, realising how much the phone was eating into limited time before the deadline.

qa.q: Which of Ujjwal's choices could others try, and why do they work?
qa.a: Keeping one news source once a day and removing feeds from the home screen work because they cut the default pull without banning everything.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see the changes in the flat?
qa.a: Tenzin had to shift drum practice, but got earplugs and a flatmate who came to the gig and was fully present.

grounding: Under a deadline in a noisy flat, a young translator chooses which apps and news to keep deliberately instead of by default.

passage:
Pooja noticed it on a Sunday in Chennai: she had spent forty minutes in bed watching strangers' kitchen makeovers, and she didn't even want a new kitchen.

She sat up. "Darshan, how many apps do you think I actually chose?"

Her husband looked up from the newspaper. "Chose?"

"Most of them I downloaded because someone said to. Or they came on the phone."

That week she went through them one by one. For each, she asked: do I use this on purpose, or does it use me? She kept the maps, banking, the family chat and a language-learning app she genuinely liked. She deleted the video app and switched her screen to greyscale in the evenings.

She also subscribed to the paper newspaper Darshan read, instead of three news feeds.

The first few evenings, she kept reaching for the phone and finding nothing interesting. By the third week, she was reading a novel on the balcony, and Darshan had quietly started doing greyscale too.

qa.q: What was Pooja watching for forty minutes in bed?
qa.a: She was watching strangers' kitchen makeovers.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel during the first few evenings after deleting the apps?
qa.a: Pooja felt restless and a bit bored, still reaching for the phone out of habit and finding nothing.

qa.q: What question did Pooja use to choose her tools, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked whether she uses each app on purpose or it uses her, which helps separate chosen tools from default ones.

qa.q: How is Darshan affected by Pooja's changes?
qa.a: Darshan was puzzled at first, but gets a companion for the newspaper and quietly copies the greyscale habit himself.

grounding: A young woman reviews her apps and news sources and keeps only the ones she uses on purpose.

passage:
"Why are you leaving the college alumni group?" Sunaina asked, peering at Gurleen's phone.

"Because it sends two hundred messages a day and I read none of them."

"But what if you miss something?"

"Then someone will tell me. That's what you're for."

Sunaina laughed. "Rude. What else?"

"Notifications off for everything except calls, and messages from you, Mumma and my manager. News only in the morning, one site. And the shopping apps are going."

"The shopping apps? You love the sales."

"That's the problem. I don't need anything. They just tell me I do."

Sunaina was quiet for a moment. "I feel anxious just hearing this."

"I did too, last week. I thought I'd feel cut off." Gurleen put the phone face down on the table. "Mostly I feel like I have my evenings back."

"Can you show me how to do the notification thing?"

"Only if you promise not to send me two hundred messages."

qa.q: Which notifications did Gurleen keep on?
qa.a: Gurleen kept notifications for calls and for messages from Sunaina, Mumma and the manager.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel hearing about Gurleen's changes?
qa.a: Sunaina felt anxious, worried about missing things, even just hearing the plan.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen delete the shopping apps, and what could a friend learn from that?
qa.a: Gurleen realised the apps created a feeling of needing things, so a friend could ask whether an app serves a real need or creates one.

qa.q: What is it like for Sunaina to watch Gurleen make these choices?
qa.a: Sunaina is first surprised and anxious, then curious enough to ask for help setting up her own notifications.

passage:
Two years ago I had eighty-three apps on my phone. I checked it one hundred and fifty times a day; the phone told me so. I felt busy and scattered all the time, and I couldn't read a book for more than five minutes.
My friend Rajni had quietly deleted most of hers and seemed calmer. I asked how. She said, "I didn't quit. I chose."
So I tried her method. For each app, I asked: does it serve something I value, like my work, family, health or learning? If not, delete. If yes, when do I use it? I kept maps, banking, one messaging app, and a reading app. Social media moved to the laptop, twice a week.
The first week I kept picking up the phone for nothing. By the third, I'd read a whole novel.
I'm Vandana. I still use technology all the time. I just decide what it's for.

qa.q: How many apps did Vandana have two years ago?
qa.a: Eighty-three apps.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel before changing the phone?
qa.a: Vandana felt restless and frustrated, busy and scattered all the time, unable to focus on a book.

qa.q: What question did Vandana use to decide which apps to keep, and why does it work?
qa.a: Whether the app serves something valued, like work, family, health or learning, because it replaces habit with conscious choice.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel seeing Vandana's change?
qa.a: Rajni would probably feel pleased that sharing her method helped a friend feel calmer.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing technology and information deliberately rather than by default.

passage:
Team note. Jagdish, design team manager.
Last quarter, my team of six spent most of the day in chat and meetings. Shreya, 25, our youngest designer, came to me with a proposal: two "deep work" afternoons a week, no meetings, chat on "do not disturb", urgent issues by phone only.
She'd tracked her own week: fifty-two chat interruptions a day, the longest focus stretch twenty minutes. She looked nervous presenting it, as if I might think she was lazy.
We tried it for a month. At first people felt anxious about missing messages. By week three, two designers finished projects that had dragged for months. Shreya also suggested we move project updates to a written weekly note instead of a meeting.
Not everyone loved it. Our sales liaison grumbled. But we've kept it, and I've asked Shreya to present the idea to other teams.

qa.q: How many chat interruptions a day did Shreya track?
qa.a: Fifty-two chat interruptions a day.

qa.q: How did Shreya seem to feel while presenting her proposal?
qa.a: Shreya seemed nervous, worried the manager might think she was lazy.

qa.q: What made Shreya's proposal persuasive?
qa.a: She brought data from her own week, suggested a clear, limited experiment, and offered a simple replacement for status meetings.

qa.q: How might the sales liaison see the new afternoons?
qa.a: The sales liaison may feel frustrated at slower replies, and might need a clear way to reach the team urgently.

grounding: Shows a young professional helping her team choose tools and communication deliberately rather than by default.

passage:
Day 30
Sarika here. The app audit is done.
A month ago Aparna Didi challenged me: write down every app I opened and how I felt after. I thought it would be boring. It was shocking.
Short-video app: forty minutes a day, felt worse every time. News app: checked eleven times a day, learned nothing new after the first. Shopping app: opened when bored, bought things I didn't need.
Apps I felt better after: my language-learning one, the one where I call Nani, my notes app.
So I deleted the video and shopping apps. I moved news to one check at lunch, from one proper newspaper site. I set my phone to greyscale after nine.
It's not perfect. I reinstalled the video app on day twelve and deleted it again on day thirteen. But I feel like the phone is mine again.

qa.q: How many times a day did Sarika check the news app?
qa.a: Eleven times a day.

qa.q: How does Sarika feel at the end of the audit?
qa.a: Sarika feels calmer and more in control, like the phone is Sarika's own again, despite a slip on day twelve.

qa.q: Why was tracking how each app made Sarika feel a useful method?
qa.a: It showed which apps served Sarika and which drained time or mood, so choices were based on evidence, not habit.

qa.q: How might Aparna Didi feel reading this diary entry?
qa.a: Aparna Didi would probably feel proud and pleased that the challenge worked.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult auditing technology use and choosing an information diet deliberately.
